headline: Pluto Shows Signs of Hidden Liquid Activity
meta_description: NASA's New Horizons spacecraft found evidence that liquid nitrogen may still be flowing beneath Pluto's frozen surface, revealing surprising geological activit…
summary_short: Scientists discovered the first signs that liquid nitrogen may be seeping onto Pluto's surface, suggesting the distant dwarf planet is far more geologically active than…
body:
Pluto, long considered a frozen, geologically dead world, may harbor hidden liquid activity beneath its surface. NASA's New Horizons spacecraft has revealed the first evidence that liquid nitrogen is likely seeping through cracks in Sputnik Planitia, the enormous heart-shaped glacier that dominates much of the dwarf planet. This discovery suggests that Pluto has undergone geological change in recent times—perhaps within the past million years—challenging our understanding of this distant, frozen realm at the edge of our solar system.

The clue came from dark markings and patches discovered in the northern region of Sputnik Planitia, a glacier larger than Texas and Oklahoma combined. Researchers, led by Southwest Research Institute's Dr. Alan Stern, compared these patterns with similar features on Greenland's ice sheet, where dark lines appear where liquid water emerges from beneath the ice. Computer models suggest that nitrogen ice at Sputnik Planitia's base—several kilometers deep—can melt under pressure and rise through narrow channels to the surface, much like water moving through geysers, before eventually evaporating in Pluto's harsh conditions.

What makes this discovery particularly striking is its scope. More than half of Pluto remains unmapped at high resolution, meaning similar activity could be occurring in other regions of the dwarf planet. The same mechanism might also explain geysers observed on Triton, Neptune's largest moon, suggesting that subtle geological processes operate throughout the distant solar system. For scientists studying worlds far beyond Earth, Pluto continues to deliver surprises—reminding us that even the frozen edges of our solar system remain dynamic and full of secrets waiting to be uncovered.
quick_facts: Sputnik Planitia glacier is larger than Texas and Oklahoma combined
Dark surface features may be less than one million years old
Liquid nitrogen rises from several kilometers beneath the ice
NASA's New Horizons spacecraft provided the observations
Over half of Pluto remains unmapped at high resolution
